title: Design a fixed-capacity cache that evicts the least recently used entry when full, supporting get and put in constant time.
shortTitle: Design an LRU Cache (Least Recently Used)
keyPoints: An LRU cache evicts the entry that was accessed longest ago when it reaches capacity
A HashMap gives O(1) lookup and a doubly linked list maintains recency order
On get, unlink the node from its current position and move it to the front of the list
On put, create or update the node at the front; if over capacity, remove the tail node and its map entry
Sentinel head and tail nodes eliminate null-check edge cases in the link and unlink logic
Java's LinkedHashMap with access-order true and removeEldestEntry is a production shortcut
The hand-rolled version is not thread-safe; use Caffeine or ConcurrentHashMap wrappers in production

s1_definition.oneliner: A HashMap for O(1) lookup plus a doubly linked list for recency order gives constant-time get and put with least-recently-used eviction.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **LRU cache** – a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the entry accessed longest ago when a new entry arrives and the cache is full.
- **HashMap** – maps every key to its doubly linked list node, giving O(1) lookup.
- **Doubly linked list** – orders nodes by recency; the most recently used node sits at the front and the least recently used sits at the tail.
- **Sentinel nodes** – dummy head and tail nodes that simplify link and unlink operations by removing null checks.
- **Eviction** – when the cache exceeds capacity, the tail node (least recently used) is removed from both the list and the map.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps only the ten most recently viewed customer profiles on a fast desk because fetching the full archive is slow. Every time a clerk views a profile, she moves that folder to the front of the desk. When a new profile is needed and the desk is full, she removes the folder at the very back, the one nobody has touched for the longest time. A card index on the side tells her instantly where each folder sits so she never searches the desk.

sections.s6_takeaway:
An LRU cache holds a fixed number of entries and evicts the one accessed longest ago when a new entry arrives and the cache is full. The design challenge is making both get and put run in constant time, and the classic solution pairs two data structures. A HashMap gives O(1) lookup from key to node, and a doubly linked list orders the nodes by recency with the most recently used at the front and the least recently used at the tail.

On a get, I look up the key in the map, unlink the node from its current position, and re-insert it right after the head sentinel to mark it most recently used. On a put, if the key exists I update its value and move it to the front. If it is new, I create a node, insert it after the head, and add it to the map. If the size exceeds capacity, I remove the tail node and delete its key from the map. Sentinel head and tail nodes make the splice logic clean because there are no null edge cases.

In the National Bank of India mobile app, I used this pattern to cache recently requested account balances. The database round-trip was too slow for the high-traffic balance endpoint, so we kept recently requested balances in memory. When the cache was full, the balance nobody had asked for in the longest time was evicted. Both the read and the insert were constant time, which was critical on that hot path.

The production recommendation is to use Java's `LinkedHashMap` in access-order mode with `removeEldestEntry` overridden, or a library like Caffeine for concurrent access and better eviction policies. I implement the HashMap-plus-doubly-linked-list by hand in interviews to demonstrate that I understand the mechanics, but I always name the production-ready option.

Remember one sentence: a HashMap for O(1) lookup plus a doubly linked list for O(1) reordering gives constant-time get and put with least-recently-used eviction.
